In the World Cup finals, more than 23%, nearly a quarter, of the players were not born in the country they represent, with both the ratio and the number reaching historic highs. Among the 48 participating teams, eight teams have the majority of their players born abroad. The Netherlands' Caribbean constituent country Curaçao, with a population smaller than Wan Chai, has only its most valuable player, Sheffield United's Chinese-descendant Tahith Chong, born locally, with all other players coming from the Netherlands itself. The 'David vs Goliath' contrast in the World Cup is not only reflected from the fans' viewing perspective, but also in the challenges FIFA faces in simultaneously leveraging star players and minnows to boost viewership. This tournament has been rife with controversy, with fans mocking favoured stars as 'FIFA Boy', and multiple national teams filing appeals to FIFA over officiating standards after matches. All of this reflects that, despite FIFA achieving record revenues from this World Cup, the confidence of the tournament's most important participants—the players—in the organisation is wavering.

For fans, when they recall the classic matches of the 2026 World Cup in the future, it may not be the final, but the thrilling 3-2 elimination match in which defending champions Argentina faced Cape Verde. The previously unknown 40-year-old Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha repeatedly blocked shots from football king Messi, becoming an overnight sensation, and now has nearly 30 million followers. Before the previous World Cup, FIFA sent a letter to all participating teams, earnestly requesting them to 'let football be the protagonist' and not let football be drawn into any ideological or political struggles. At that time, the World Cup was still hosted by a single country, with 32 participating teams. The next World Cup will celebrate its centenary and will unprecedentedly span three continents and six countries.
